\chapter{Bounded lifts and strong continuous duals of the original-zeta
coefficient}\label{bounded-lifts-and-strong-continuous-duals-of-the-original-zeta-coefficient}

Independent derivation, 24 September 2026. Proof locators SDT0--SDT9.

\section{SDT0. Actual input, source stage, and the assertion
proved}\label{sdt0.-actual-input-source-stage-and-the-assertion-proved}

This calculation starts on the coefficient spaces already constructed in
CSP and CDI. The supporting datum remains
\(\tau\langle Z_1;\mathrm{no}\ Z_2\rangle\). All vector operations,
seminorms, analytic coordinates, quotients and duals below belong to
those reconstructed arithmetic coefficients. None is an operation or a
newly assigned metric on that supporting datum.

The complete construction and its correction history were read for the
preceding CS and CSB calculations. For this continuation the current
construction guide, active-target and correction-precedence passages,
and the full verbatim WU061--WU062 were reread. The mathematical input
actually read here is
\href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/zeta-function-research-reader/blob/main/workbenches/splitzero-tandem/continuations/20260924-cohomology-weight-and-character-lifts/gct-weight-control/proofs/CC_CONTINUOUS_DUAL_INDEPENDENT.md}{CDI0--CDI3
and CDI8--CDI12}, together with the exact coefficient definitions in
\href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/zeta-function-research-reader/blob/main/workbenches/splitzero-tandem/continuations/20260924-cohomology-weight-and-character-lifts/gct-weight-control/proofs/CC_SPHERE_PULLBACK_AND_NORMAL_DIRECTION.md}{CSP0--CSP1}.
The exact-image results
\href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/zeta-function-research-reader/blob/main/workbenches/splitzero-tandem/continuations/20260924-cohomology-weight-and-character-lifts/gct-weight-control/proofs/EXACT_SCHWARTZ_SUMMATION_IMAGE.md}{SSI1--SSI7}
and
\href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/zeta-function-research-reader/blob/main/workbenches/splitzero-tandem/continuations/20260924-cohomology-weight-and-character-lifts/gct-weight-control/proofs/EXACT_SCHWARTZ_IMAGE_INDEPENDENT_CHECK.md}{ESI0--ESI9}
were read during the preceding calculation and are retained with their
actual proof status.

The underlying human source is Connes--Consani, \emph{Schemes over
\(\mathbb F_1\) and zeta functions},
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.2024v3}{arXiv:0903.2024v3}, §5. Its
original author TeX, retained at
sources/CC\_0903\_2024\_v3/author\_source/announc3.tex, was previously
read at lines 1376--1667. This note strengthens the topology of the
already proved coefficient comparison; it is not a new reading of the
entire human source or an identification with a Deligne dualizing
complex.

Retain exactly \[
S=\left\{f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R;\mathbb C):
f(-v)=f(v),\ f(0)=0,\ \int_{\mathbb R}f(v)\,dv=0\right\},
\] \[
A=\left\{a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R_{>0}):
p_{N,j}(a)<\infty\ \text{for every }N,j\ge0\right\},
\quad
p_{N,j}(a)=\sup_{u>0}(u^N+u^{-N})|(u\partial_u)^ja(u)|,
\] \[
\Sigma f(u)=2\sum_{n\ge1}f(nu),\qquad
J=\Sigma S,\qquad Q=A/J,\qquad q:A\longrightarrow Q.
\tag{SDT0.1}
\] Here \(N,j\) are nonnegative integers and the topology on \(A\) is
the topology of all the displayed seminorms. SSI and ESI prove that
\(J\) is closed and that \(\Sigma:S\to J\) is a topological isomorphism.

We prove all of the following for these actual spaces:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Every bounded subset of \(A\), and every bounded subset of \(Q\), has
  compact closure.
\item
  Every compact subset of \(Q\) is the image of a compact subset of
  \(A\); consequently every bounded subset of \(Q\) has a bounded lift.
\item
  The continuous bijection in CDI3.3 is a topological isomorphism \[
  q':Q'_\beta\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }J^\perp\subset A'_\beta.
  \tag{SDT0.2}
  \]
\item
  The evaluation maps identify the strong biduals of \(A\) and \(Q\)
  with their original topologies.
\item
  The span of all actual nontrivial-zero jet functionals is strongly
  dense in the entire continuous dual of the original-zeta quotient.
\end{enumerate}

No nuclearity theorem or general bounded-lifting assertion is assumed.
The compactness and lifting arguments are constructed below. In
particular the statement is not deduced merely from the fact that a map
of Fréchet spaces is onto.

\section{SDT1. The original weighted topology and its quotient
seminorms}\label{sdt1.-the-original-weighted-topology-and-its-quotient-seminorms}

Use the analytic change of variable \(x=\log u\) only on \(A\), writing
\[
g(x)=a(e^x),\qquad
w_n(x)=e^{nx}+e^{-nx},\qquad
P_n(a)=\max_{0\le j\le n}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
w_n(x)|g^{(j)}(x)|.
\tag{SDT1.1}
\] Thus \(P_n=\max_{j\le n}p_{n,j}\) is expressed in the original
seminorms, including both summands of the weight. No summand has been
removed. The sequence \(P_n\) is increasing: \(w_n(x)=2\cosh(nx)\) is
increasing with \(n\ge0\), and the derivative range increases. For every
\(N,j\), choosing \(n\ge\max(N,j)\) gives \[
p_{N,j}\le P_n.
\tag{SDT1.2}
\] Conversely every \(P_n\) is a finite maximum of defining seminorms.
Hence this is exactly the original topology. Each \(P_n\) is a norm on
\(A\).

For completeness, a sequence Cauchy in every \(P_n\) is Cauchy with
every derivative uniformly on every compact interval in \(x\). The
corresponding uniform limits have the derivative compatibility obtained
by integrating each first derivative on a compact interval. Inducting
over derivatives gives a smooth limit \(g\). For every \(n\), the
weighted derivatives are uniform Cauchy functions on the whole real
axis, so their uniform limits are precisely \(w_n g^{(j)}\). Set
\(a(u)=g(\log u)\). Then \(P_n(a-a_k)\to0\) and \(P_n(a)<\infty\). This
proves that \(A\) is complete. The metric \[
d_A(a,b)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{-n-1}
\min\{1,P_n(a-b)\}
\tag{SDT1.3}
\] generates its topology. Thus \(A\) is a Hausdorff Fréchet space.

Define actual quotient seminorms \[
\overline P_n(q(a))=\inf_{j\in J}P_n(a+j).
\tag{SDT1.4}
\] They are well defined, increasing, and subadditive, and they satisfy
\[
q\{P_n<\varepsilon\}=\{\overline P_n<\varepsilon\}.
\tag{SDT1.5}
\] The equality uses the strict inequality: an infimum below
\(\varepsilon\) supplies a representative with \(P_n<\varepsilon\).
These sets generate exactly the quotient topology. Images of open sets
under \(q\) are open because their inverse images are the open sets
\(U+J\).

If all \(\overline P_n(y)\) vanish, a representative \(a\) of \(y\) can
be approximated by elements of \(J\) in every neighborhood defined by
some \(P_n\). Thus \(a\in\overline J=J\) and \(y=0\). The quotient is
therefore Hausdorff.

We also give its completeness argument. Let \((y_\ell)\) be Cauchy for
every \(\overline P_n\). Choose a subsequence \((y_{\ell_k})_{k\ge1}\)
so that \[
\overline P_k(y_{\ell_{k+1}}-y_{\ell_k})<2^{-k-1}.
\] Choose \(b_k\in A\) with \[
q(b_k)=y_{\ell_{k+1}}-y_{\ell_k},\qquad P_k(b_k)<2^{-k}.
\tag{SDT1.6}
\] For every fixed \(m\), the tail from \(k\ge m\) is absolutely
summable in \(P_m\), since \(P_m\le P_k\). The series
\(\sum_{k\ge1}b_k\) therefore converges in \(A\). Adding any
representative of \(y_{\ell_1}\), then applying \(q\), gives a limit of
the chosen subsequence. The original Cauchy sequence has that same
limit. The metric obtained from (SDT1.3) by replacing \(P_n\) by
\(\overline P_n\) is complete, so \(Q\) is Fréchet.

This proof uses the quotient's actual closed kernel, not a completion in
which nonzero quotient classes are discarded.

\section{SDT2. A finite-net estimate with the two original weights
retained}\label{sdt2.-a-finite-net-estimate-with-the-two-original-weights-retained}

Fix \(n\ge0\) and \(M>0\). Consider \[
\mathcal U_{n+1,M}=\{a\in A:P_{n+1}(a)\le M\}.
\tag{SDT2.1}
\] This set need not be bounded in the full Fréchet topology. We prove
the exact assertion needed: it is totally bounded for the single norm
\(P_n\).

For all \(x\in\mathbb R\), \[
\frac{w_n(x)}{w_{n+1}(x)}
=\frac{e^{nx}+e^{-nx}}{e^{(n+1)x}+e^{-(n+1)x}}
\le 2e^{-|x|}.
\tag{SDT2.2}
\] Indeed the numerator is at most \(2e^{n|x|}\), while the denominator
is at least \(e^{(n+1)|x|}\). If \(a,b\in\mathcal U_{n+1,M}\), then for
\(0\le j\le n\), \[
\sup_{|x|>T}w_n(x)|g_a^{(j)}(x)-g_b^{(j)}(x)|
\le 4M e^{-T}.
\tag{SDT2.3}
\] For a prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(T>0\) with
\(4Me^{-T}<\varepsilon/2\).

On \([-T,T]\), each \(g_a^{(j)}\), \(j\le n+1\), has absolute value at
most \(M/2\), because \(w_{n+1}\ge2\). The functions \(g_a^{(j)}\),
\(j\le n\), are therefore Lipschitz with constant at most \(M/2\). Put
\(W=w_n(T)\). Choose a finite mesh of \([-T,T]\) with every point at
distance at most \(\delta\) from a mesh point, where \[
0<\delta<\frac{\varepsilon}{4MW}.
\tag{SDT2.4}
\] At every mesh point, quantize each of the finitely many complex
numbers \(g_a^{(j)}\), \(j\le n\), to a finite set with error at most
\(\eta\), where \[
0<\eta<\frac{\varepsilon}{8W}.
\tag{SDT2.5}
\] The bound \(M/2\) makes that quantization finite. There are finitely
many resulting joint codes. For each occupied code choose one function
\(b\) in the set with that code. If \(a\) has the same code, the two
Lipschitz bounds and the two quantization errors give \[
\sup_{|x|\le T}w_n(x)|g_a^{(j)}(x)-g_b^{(j)}(x)|
\le W(M\delta+2\eta)<\varepsilon/2
\quad(0\le j\le n).
\tag{SDT2.6}
\] Combining (SDT2.3) and (SDT2.6) proves \(P_n(a-b)<\varepsilon\). The
finitely many selected \(b\)'s form a finite \(P_n\)-net. For \(M=0\)
the set is the singleton zero, so the same conclusion holds.

Every bounded \(B\subset A\) has a finite bound for \(P_{n+1}\), for
each \(n\). It is therefore totally bounded for every \(P_n\). To see
that this is total boundedness for \(d_A\), first make the tail
\(\sum_{n>N}2^{-n-1}\) small, and then use a finite sufficiently small
\(P_N\)-net to control all terms with \(n\le N\). Since \(A\) is
complete, \(\overline B\) is compact.

The final metric fact can be verified directly: a totally bounded metric
space permits extraction of a Cauchy subsequence from every sequence by
successive finite covers of radii tending to zero; completeness supplies
its limit. Thus its closed completion is compact. No additional locally
convex compactness theorem is needed.

\section{SDT3. Bounded quotient sets have compact
closure}\label{sdt3.-bounded-quotient-sets-have-compact-closure}

Let \(B\subset Q\) be bounded in the actual quotient topology. For each
\(n\), put \[
M_n=\sup_{y\in B}\overline P_{n+1}(y)<\infty.
\tag{SDT3.1}
\] For each \(y\in B\) choose a representative \(a_y\in A\) with \[
q(a_y)=y,\qquad P_{n+1}(a_y)<M_n+1.
\tag{SDT3.2}
\] These choices are made separately for the present index \(n\); no
assertion that they form a single Fréchet-bounded set is used here.

By SDT2, the set of these representatives admits a finite \(P_n\)-net.
Applying \(q\) and using \(\overline P_n(q(a))\le P_n(a)\) gives a
finite \(\overline P_n\)-net for \(B\). Thus \(B\) is totally bounded in
every quotient seminorm and hence in the complete quotient metric of
SDT1. Its closure is compact: \[
\boxed{B\subset Q\ \text{bounded}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\overline B^{\,Q}\ \text{compact}.}
\tag{SDT3.3}
\] The same statement for \(A\) was proved in SDT2. In the usual
terminology these Fréchet spaces are Montel: they are barrelled, and
their closed bounded sets are compact. The barrelled assertion follows
from the Baire argument supplied in SDT6. No quotient-stability
assertion about general Montel spaces is required here.

Closed subspaces of \(A\), including \(J\), have the same
bounded-compact property by intersection with their closed ambient
subspace. Finite products of such spaces retain the property, because
projections of a bounded set have compact closures and its closure is a
closed subset of the product of those compact sets. In particular the
actual graph coefficient \(Z=J\oplus E_+\oplus E_-\) also has this
property.

\section{SDT4. Constructive compact lifting through the actual
quotient}\label{sdt4.-constructive-compact-lifting-through-the-actual-quotient}

We prove a compact lifting statement for this quotient directly. The
argument works for a quotient of any Fréchet space by a closed subspace,
but its hypotheses and construction will remain explicit.

For \(n\ge1\), define \[
U_n=\{a\in A:P_n(a)<2^{-n}\},\qquad
W_n=\{y\in Q:\overline P_n(y)<2^{-n-1}\},
\] \[
C_n=\{y\in Q:\overline P_n(y)\le2^{-n-1}\}.
\tag{SDT4.1}
\] Then \(C_n\) is closed, \(W_n\) is an open neighborhood of zero, \[
\overline{W_n}\subset C_n\subset q(U_n).
\tag{SDT4.2}
\] The last inclusion follows from the strict gap \(2^{-n-1}<2^{-n}\)
and (SDT1.5).

Let \(K\subset Q\) be compact and nonempty. Choose
\(y_{0,1},\ldots,y_{0,r_0}\in K\) such that the translates
\(y_{0,i}+W_1\) cover \(K\). Choose arbitrary lifts \(a_{0,i}\in A\)
with \(q(a_{0,i})=y_{0,i}\), and put \[
F_0=\{a_{0,1},\ldots,a_{0,r_0}\},\qquad
K_1=\bigcup_{i=1}^{r_0}\bigl((K-y_{0,i})\cap C_1\bigr).
\tag{SDT4.3}
\] Each intersection is a closed subset of a compact translate of \(K\).
Hence \(K_1\) is compact and lies in \(C_1\subset q(U_1)\). Every
\(y\in K\) has a representation \(y=q(a_0)+r_1\) with \(a_0\in F_0\) and
\(r_1\in K_1\).

Inductively suppose the compact set \(K_n\subset C_n\) is constructed.
Choose finitely many centers \(y_{n,i}\in K_n\) whose translates
\(y_{n,i}+W_{n+1}\) cover \(K_n\). Since \(K_n\subset q(U_n)\), choose
lifts \[
q(a_{n,i})=y_{n,i},\qquad a_{n,i}\in U_n.
\] Define \[
F_n=\{a_{n,i}\}_i,\qquad
K_{n+1}=\bigcup_i\bigl((K_n-y_{n,i})\cap C_{n+1}\bigr).
\tag{SDT4.4}
\] Again \(K_{n+1}\) is compact and contained in \(C_{n+1}\). The finite
cover ensures that every residual \(r_n\in K_n\) can be written \[
r_n=q(a_n)+r_{n+1},\qquad
a_n\in F_n,\quad r_{n+1}\in K_{n+1}.
\tag{SDT4.5}
\] These finite sets are nonempty: each chosen center gives residual
zero in the next residual set. Thus the displayed finite products are
nonempty when \(K\) is nonempty.

Every choice from the product \(\prod_{n=0}^\infty F_n\) has a
convergent sum in \(A\). For a fixed \(m\) and \(N\ge\max(m,1)\), its
tails satisfy the uniform estimate \[
P_m\left(\sum_{n>N}a_n\right)
\le\sum_{n>N}P_m(a_n)
\le\sum_{n>N}2^{-n}=2^{-N}.
\tag{SDT4.6}
\] Completeness of \(A\) proves existence of each sum. The sum map \[
\Psi:\prod_{n=0}^\infty F_n\longrightarrow A,\qquad
\Psi((a_n))=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n
\tag{SDT4.7}
\] is continuous: finite partial sums are continuous and (SDT4.6)
controls the remainder uniformly in every defining seminorm.

The product of these finite discrete sets is compact. One can see this
without an uncountable-product assertion: give it the metric recording
the first coordinate at which two sequences differ; a diagonal
subsequence argument gives a convergent subsequence from every sequence.
Its image \[
B_K^*=\Psi\left(\prod_{n=0}^\infty F_n\right)
\tag{SDT4.8}
\] is therefore compact.

For any \(y\in K\), choose a compatible residual path using (SDT4.3) and
(SDT4.5). After stage \(N\), \[
y-q\left(\sum_{n=0}^N a_n\right)=r_{N+1}\in C_{N+1}.
\] For \(N+1\ge m\), \[
\overline P_m(r_{N+1})
\le\overline P_{N+1}(r_{N+1})
\le2^{-N-2}.
\tag{SDT4.9}
\] Thus the residual tends to zero in \(Q\), and continuity of \(q\)
gives \(q(\Psi((a_n)))=y\). This proves \(K\subset q(B_K^*)\). The
compact set \[
B_K=B_K^*\cap q^{-1}(K)
\tag{SDT4.10}
\] then satisfies \(q(B_K)=K\). The intersection is closed in \(B_K^*\),
because the compact set \(K\) is closed in the Hausdorff space \(Q\).
Empty \(K\) has the empty lift.

We have constructed, rather than assumed, \[
\boxed{K\subset Q\ \text{compact}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists B_K\subset A\ \text{compact with }q(B_K)=K.}
\tag{SDT4.11}
\] The construction supplies a compact set of lifts. It makes no
assertion that \(q\) has a continuous linear section, and it does not
choose a new topology on either coefficient.

\section{SDT5. Bounded lifting and equality of the strong-dual
topologies}\label{sdt5.-bounded-lifting-and-equality-of-the-strong-dual-topologies}

Let \(B\subset Q\) be bounded. SDT3 gives the compact closure
\(K=\overline B\). Lift \(K\) by SDT4 and define \[
\widetilde B=B_K\cap q^{-1}(B).
\tag{SDT5.1}
\] This set need not be closed or compact, but it is a subset of the
compact set \(B_K\), hence is bounded. Every \(y\in B\) has a preimage
in it. Therefore \[
\boxed{q(\widetilde B)=B,\qquad \widetilde B\subset A\ \text{bounded}.}
\tag{SDT5.2}
\] Compact sets are bounded because every continuous seminorm has a
finite maximum on them; the seminorm characterization of boundedness
then gives the assertion for their subsets.

For a locally convex space \(E\), retain the strong-dual seminorms \[
p_D(\lambda)=\sup_{x\in D}|\lambda(x)|,
\qquad D\subset E\ \text{bounded}.
\tag{SDT5.3}
\] CDI1 proves the algebraic identification \(q'Q'=J^\perp\). If
\(C\subset A\) is bounded, then \(q(C)\) is bounded and \[
p_C(q'\mu)=p_{q(C)}(\mu).
\tag{SDT5.4}
\] This proves continuity of \(q':Q'_\beta\to A'_\beta\). Conversely,
for every bounded \(B\subset Q\), choose its exact bounded lift from
(SDT5.2). Then \[
p_B(\mu)=p_{\widetilde B}(q'\mu).
\tag{SDT5.5}
\] Every defining strong seminorm on \(Q'\) is thus the restriction of a
defining strong seminorm from \(A'\). Equations (SDT5.4) and (SDT5.5)
prove \[
\boxed{Q'_\beta\xrightarrow[\mu\mapsto\mu\circ q]{\ \sim\ }
(J^\perp,\text{subspace topology from }A'_\beta).}
\tag{SDT5.6}
\] The annihilator \(J^\perp\) is closed, being the intersection of the
continuous evaluation kernels at \(j\in J\). This resolves the specific
topology left open in CDI3.2--CDI3.3.

No openness conclusion for the separate restriction map
\(A'_\beta\to J'_\beta\) is needed for (SDT5.6), and no such conclusion
is asserted here.

\section{SDT6. The full strong bidual is the original
coefficient}\label{sdt6.-the-full-strong-bidual-is-the-original-coefficient}

Let \(E\) be \(A\) or \(Q\), with exactly the topology already proved.
The argument also applies to the closed subspace \(J\) and the
finite-product graph coefficient \(Z\) from SDT3.

First let \(\Lambda:E'_\beta\to\mathbb C\) be continuous and linear.
Continuity at zero gives finitely many bounded sets
\(B_1,\ldots,B_r\subset E\) and a finite constant \(C\) such that \[
|\Lambda(\lambda)|\le C\max_i p_{B_i}(\lambda)
=p_{C B}(\lambda),\qquad B=\bigcup_i B_i.
\tag{SDT6.1}
\] If \(C=0\), then \(\Lambda=0\). Otherwise let \[
D=\overline{\operatorname{aconv}(CB)}^{\,E},
\tag{SDT6.2}
\] where the absolutely convex hull consists of finite sums
\(\sum_i c_i b_i\) with \(b_i\in CB\) and \(\sum_i|c_i|\le1\). Every
continuous seminorm is bounded on \(D\) by its supremum on \(CB\). Thus
\(D\) is bounded. By SDT2 or SDT3 it is compact, as well as closed and
absolutely convex. Equation (SDT6.1) becomes \[
|\Lambda(\lambda)|\le\sup_{x\in D}|\lambda(x)|.
\tag{SDT6.3}
\]

For any finite family \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r\in E'\), the vector
\((\Lambda(\lambda_1),\ldots,\Lambda(\lambda_r))\) belongs to the
compact absolutely convex set \[
\{(\lambda_1(x),\ldots,\lambda_r(x)):x\in D\}\subset\mathbb C^r.
\tag{SDT6.4}
\] Indeed, otherwise finite-dimensional real separation would give a
complex linear combination \(\lambda=\sum_i c_i\lambda_i\) whose real
value at that vector exceeds its supremum on the displayed set. Absolute
convexity identifies that supremum with the supremum of the modulus.
This contradicts (SDT6.3).

Hence the closed subsets \(\{x\in D:\lambda(x)=\Lambda(\lambda)\}\),
indexed by \(\lambda\in E'\), have the finite intersection property.
Compactness of \(D\) gives \(x\in D\) with \[
\Lambda(\lambda)=\lambda(x)\quad\text{for every }\lambda\in E'.
\tag{SDT6.5}
\] Hahn--Banach separation of points in the Hausdorff locally convex
space \(E\) makes \(x\) unique. Therefore \[
(E'_\beta)'=E
\tag{SDT6.6}
\] under the specified evaluation map, as vector spaces.

We prove equality of topologies as well. A bounded set
\(M\subset E'_\beta\) is pointwise bounded, since each singleton
\(\{x\}\subset E\) is bounded. Put \[
C_k=\{x\in E:\sup_{\lambda\in M}|\lambda(x)|\le k\},
\qquad k=1,2,\ldots.
\tag{SDT6.7}
\] Each \(C_k\) is closed and their union is \(E\). The Baire theorem
for the complete metric space \(E\) gives an interior point \(x_0\) of
one \(C_k\). For a neighborhood \(U\) of zero with \(x_0+U\subset C_k\),
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in M}|\lambda(u)|\le2k\quad(u\in U).
\tag{SDT6.8}
\] Thus \(M\) is equicontinuous, and the seminorm
\(x\mapsto\sup_{\lambda\in M}|\lambda(x)|\) is continuous on \(E\). This
proves continuity of evaluation into the strong bidual.

For the reverse topology, let \(P\) be any continuous seminorm on \(E\),
and set \[
M_P=\{\lambda\in E':|\lambda(x)|\le P(x)\text{ for all }x\in E\}.
\tag{SDT6.9}
\] For every bounded \(B\subset E\), \[
\sup_{\lambda\in M_P}p_B(\lambda)\le\sup_{x\in B}P(x)<\infty.
\] Hence \(M_P\) is bounded in \(E'_\beta\). Complex Hahn--Banach,
applied to each one-dimensional span, gives \[
P(x)=\sup_{\lambda\in M_P}|\lambda(x)|.
\tag{SDT6.10}
\] Every original continuous seminorm is therefore a strong-bidual
seminorm. Together with (SDT6.5)--(SDT6.8), this proves the topological
isomorphism \[
\boxed{E\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }(E'_\beta)'_\beta,\qquad
x\longmapsto(\lambda\mapsto\lambda(x)).}
\tag{SDT6.11}
\]

For the terminology used in SDT3, the same Baire argument proves that
\(E\) is barrelled. If \(C\subset E\) is a closed, balanced, convex,
absorbing set, then \(E=\bigcup_{k\ge1}kC\). Baire gives an interior
point of some \(kC\); differences of two points in a small neighborhood
of that point lie in \(2kC\). Balanced convexity then makes \(C\) a
neighborhood of zero. This proves the barrelled property from its
definition.

\section{SDT7. Actual zero jets are strongly
dense}\label{sdt7.-actual-zero-jets-are-strongly-dense}

Retain the exact comparison coordinate, including its factor: \[
\mathcal M_0a(s)=\int_0^\infty a(u)u^s\frac{du}{u},
\qquad
\kappa:Q\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathcal Q=\mathcal B/\mathcal I,
\qquad
\kappa([a])=\left[\frac12\mathcal M_0a\right].
\tag{SDT7.1}
\] Here \(\mathcal B\) is the entire strip-Schwartz space with seminorms
\[
b_{R,M}(F)=\sup_{\substack{|\sigma|\le R\\t\in\mathbb R}}
(1+|t|)^M|F(\sigma+it)|,
\] and \[
\mathcal I=\{F\in\mathcal B:
F^{(j)}(\rho)=0\text{ for every actual nontrivial zero }\rho
\text{ of the original }\zeta,\ 0\le j<m_\rho\}.
\tag{SDT7.2}
\] These are the full actual multiplicities. The raw source identity
remains \[
\mathcal M_0\Sigma f(s)
=2\zeta(s)\int_0^\infty f(v)v^s\frac{dv}{v}
\qquad(\Re s>1).
\tag{SDT7.3}
\] SSI's continuous inverse for a raw target \(F\in\mathcal I\) is \[
f_F(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}
\frac{F(2+it)}{2\zeta(2+it)}x^{-2-it}\,dt\quad(x>0),
\] \[
f_F(-x)=f_F(x),\quad f_F(0)=0,\quad\int_{\mathbb R}f_F=0,\quad
\frac{f_F^{(2r)}(0)}{(2r)!}=\frac{F(-2r)}{2\zeta'(-2r)}
\quad(r\ge1).
\tag{SDT7.4}
\] The actual pole at 1 and trivial-zero residues are therefore not
erased by the quotient-topology argument. In (SDT7.1)'s coordinate
\(G\), the raw target is \(2G\).

Let \[
\delta_{\rho,j}([F])=F^{(j)}(\rho),\qquad
\mathscr D_{\mathrm{fin}}
=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}
\{\delta_{\rho,j}:\rho,\ 0\le j<m_\rho\}\subset\mathcal Q'.
\tag{SDT7.5}
\] Each jet is continuous: choose a circle about \(\rho\) contained in a
fixed strip and use Cauchy's formula to bound its derivative by one
\(b_{R,0}\). It vanishes on \(\mathcal I\), so factors continuously
through the quotient. Most importantly, these functionals together
separate every class: \[
\bigcap_{\rho,j}\ker\delta_{\rho,j}=\{0\}\subset\mathcal Q.
\tag{SDT7.6}
\] This is exactly the defining full-jet ideal (SDT7.2), not a finite
truncation or a simplicity assumption.

The isomorphism \(\kappa\) transfers SDT3 and SDT6 to \(\mathcal Q\).
Suppose the strong closure of \(\mathscr D_{\mathrm{fin}}\) were a
proper closed linear subspace of \(\mathcal Q'_\beta\). Hahn--Banach
separation in that Hausdorff locally convex space would give a nonzero
continuous linear functional \(\Lambda\) vanishing on that subspace. By
(SDT6.6), \(\Lambda\) is evaluation at a unique class
\(x\in\mathcal Q\). Since it vanishes on every \(\delta_{\rho,j}\),
(SDT7.6) gives \(x=0\), contrary to \(\Lambda\ne0\). Therefore \[
\boxed{\overline{\mathscr D_{\mathrm{fin}}}^{\,\beta(\mathcal Q',\mathcal Q)}
=\mathcal Q'_\beta.}
\tag{SDT7.7}
\] Equivalently, for every \(\lambda\in\mathcal Q'\), every finite
family of bounded subsets \(B_1,\ldots,B_r\subset\mathcal Q\), and every
\(\varepsilon>0\), there is a finite linear combination \(d\) of the
actual full zero jets such that \[
\max_i\sup_{x\in B_i}|\lambda(x)-d(x)|<\varepsilon.
\tag{SDT7.8}
\] This is stronger than matching finitely many evaluations. It asserts
density in the uniform-on-bounded-sets topology, with exactly the bounds
that define that topology.

For precision about completion, \(E'_\beta\) is complete for each
Fréchet \(E\) used here. Indeed a strong Cauchy net \((\lambda_\alpha)\)
is pointwise Cauchy and defines a linear limit \(\lambda\). On every
bounded set \(B\), the Cauchy estimate passes to the pointwise limit, so
convergence is uniform on \(B\). To show that \(\lambda\) is continuous,
take any sequence \(x_n\to0\) in \(E\). The compact set
\(\{0,x_1,x_2,\ldots\}\) is bounded, and uniform convergence on it makes
the restriction of \(\lambda\) a uniform limit of continuous functions.
Thus \(\lambda(x_n)\to0\). Metrizability of \(E\) turns sequential
continuity at zero into continuity. Hence \(\lambda\in E'\), and the
convergence already proved on every bounded set is strong convergence.

Consequently the Hausdorff completion of \(\mathscr D_{\mathrm{fin}}\),
with the topology induced from \(\mathcal Q'_\beta\), is canonically
\(\mathcal Q'_\beta\). This is a completion statement about jet
functionals. It does not assert that the finite-support class space
\(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}\) is dense in \(\mathcal Q\), nor that an
unproved topology on that class space is its original quotient subspace
topology.

\section{SDT8. Strong-dual cohomology and the original residue
map}\label{sdt8.-strong-dual-cohomology-and-the-original-residue-map}

Retain CDI's full endpoint and complex data: \[
E_+=\mathbb Ce_{+,0}\oplus\mathbb Ce_{+,1},\qquad
E_-=\mathbb Ce_{-,0}\oplus\mathbb Ce_{-,1},\qquad
V_\pm=S\oplus E_\pm,
\] \[
r_+(f,e)=\Sigma f,\qquad
r_-(h,e)=R\Sigma h=\Sigma\widehat h,\qquad
Ra(u)=u^{-1}a(u^{-1}),
\] \[
W=V_+\oplus V_-,\qquad
d(v_+,v_-)=r_+v_+-r_-v_-,\qquad Z=\ker d.
\tag{SDT8.1}
\] Every original endpoint line remains present. The inverse
\(\Sigma^{-1}:J\to S\) gives the continuous splittings in CDI1: \[
V_\pm\simeq E_\pm\oplus J,\qquad
W\simeq Z\oplus J,\qquad
Z\simeq J\oplus E_+\oplus E_-.
\tag{SDT8.2}
\] Finite topological direct sums transpose to finite topological direct
sums for strong duals. To check this, a bounded set has bounded
projections, and the image of a bounded set under either continuous
coordinate inclusion is bounded. The strong seminorms in each direction
are therefore bounded by finite sums or maxima of the coordinate strong
seminorms.

For the actual global complex \[
D=[W\xrightarrow d A\xrightarrow0 A]
\quad\text{in degrees }0,1,2,
\] the Hom convention
\(d_{D^\vee}^n\lambda=(-1)^{n+1}\lambda\circ d_D^{-n-1}\) gives \[
D^\vee=[A'_\beta\xrightarrow0 A'_\beta
\xrightarrow{\lambda\mapsto(r_+'\lambda,-r_-'\lambda)}
V_+'{}_\beta\oplus V_-'{}_\beta]
\quad\text{in degrees }-2,-1,0.
\tag{SDT8.3}
\] CDI1's exact transpose computation gives \(\ker d'=J^\perp\) and
\(\operatorname{im}d'=Z^\perp\). Equation (SDT5.6) identifies the kernel
topology, while (SDT8.2) identifies the quotient topology in degree
zero. Thus all three identifications are now strong topological
isomorphisms: \[
\boxed{
H^{-2}(D^\vee)=A'_\beta,\qquad
H^{-1}(D^\vee)\simeq Q'_\beta,\qquad
H^0(D^\vee)\simeq Z'_\beta.}
\tag{SDT8.4}
\] Here cohomology has its actual kernel/subspace and quotient
topologies in the displayed coefficient complex.

For each actual pole-costalk complex \(L_\pm=[V_\pm\to A\to A]\), the
same argument gives \[
\boxed{
H^{-2}(L_\pm^\vee)=A'_\beta,\qquad
H^{-1}(L_\pm^\vee)\simeq Q'_\beta,\qquad
H^0(L_\pm^\vee)\simeq E_\pm'{}_\beta.}
\tag{SDT8.5}
\] The transposed two-support maps retain their original signs: \[
A'_\beta\longrightarrow A'_\beta\oplus A'_\beta,\quad
\lambda\longmapsto(\lambda,\lambda)
\quad\text{in degree }-2,
\] \[
Q'_\beta\longrightarrow Q'_\beta\oplus Q'_\beta,\quad
\mu\longmapsto(\mu,-\mu)
\quad\text{in degree }-1.
\tag{SDT8.6}
\] They are continuous for the proved topologies. No sign is changed by
strengthening the identification in degree minus one.

Let \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}\) denote the classes whose full jet
family vanishes outside a finite set of actual zeros; every order less
than the actual multiplicity remains in each retained block. The
original-zeta residue comparison of CDI9 and
\href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/zeta-function-research-reader/blob/main/workbenches/splitzero-tandem/continuations/20260924-cohomology-weight-and-character-lifts/gct-weight-control/proofs/ORIGINAL_ZETA_RESIDUE_DUAL_AND_SUPPORT_MAPS.md}{RD2--RD4}
remains \[
\iota(G)(F)=\sum_\rho\operatorname{Res}_{s=\rho}
\frac{F(s)G(1-s)}{\zeta(s)}\,ds,
\qquad
\iota:\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
\mathscr D_{\mathrm{fin}}.
\tag{SDT8.7}
\] The sum is finite for \(G\in\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}\). Its
denominator is the original \(\zeta\). At an actual zero \(\rho\) of
multiplicity \(m\), write \[
\zeta(\rho+t)=t^m u_\rho(t),\qquad u_\rho(0)\ne0.
\] In the monomial jet bases at \(\rho\) and \(1-\rho\), its full matrix
and determinant are \[
P_{ij}=(-1)^j[t^{m-1-i-j}]\frac1{u_\rho(t)}
\quad(0\le i,j<m),\qquad
\det P=u_\rho(0)^{-m}\ne0.
\tag{SDT8.8}
\] Thus SDT7 proves that the actual image of (SDT8.7) is strongly dense.
It does not equip its domain with a new unstated topology or extend the
residue formula to an unproved infinite sum.

The unshifted arithmetic action remains \(T_a[F(s)]=[a^sF(s)]\) for
\(a>0\). Its source multiplier satisfies
\(b_{R,M}(a^sF)\le\max(a^R,a^{-R})b_{R,M}(F)\), so it is continuous on
\(\mathcal B\), preserves \(\mathcal I\), and acts continuously on
\(\mathcal Q\). The exact covariance is \[
\iota(T_aG)=a(T_{a^{-1}})'\iota(G).
\tag{SDT8.9}
\] For the normal coefficient with action \(aT_a\), the
invariant-pairing contragredient is \[
\mathsf N_a^\vee=a^{-1}(T_{a^{-1}})',\qquad
\iota(T_aG)=a^2\mathsf N_a^\vee\iota(G).
\tag{SDT8.10}
\] The strong topology does not remove either factor or the inverse
parameter. Continuous linear maps take bounded sets to bounded sets, so
all these individual transposed operators are strongly continuous. No
positivity conclusion follows from reflexivity or strong density.

One can now construct an exact completed residue receiver. Give
\(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}\) the initial locally convex topology of
\(\iota\), explicitly \[
p_B^{\mathrm{res}}(G)
=\sup_{F\in B}\left|
\sum_\rho\operatorname{Res}_{s=\rho}
\frac{F(s)G(1-s)}{\zeta(s)}\,ds\right|,
\qquad B\subset\mathcal Q\ \text{bounded}.
\tag{SDT8.11}
\] The local determinant (SDT8.8) makes this topology Hausdorff. By
definition \(\iota\) is a topological isomorphism onto
\(\mathscr D_{\mathrm{fin}}\) with its induced strong topology. SDT7
proves that the latter is dense in the complete space
\(\mathcal Q'_\beta\). Therefore the actual Hausdorff completion is \[
\boxed{
\widehat{\bigl(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}},
(p_B^{\mathrm{res}})_B\bigr)}
\xrightarrow[\ \widehat\iota\ ]{\ \sim\ }\mathcal Q'_\beta.}
\tag{SDT8.12}
\] This is a constructed residue completion. Its topology has been
specified by (SDT8.11); it is not identified with the pre-existing
subspace topology from \(\mathcal Q\).

For completeness, the ordinary-transpose comparison also has a full
formula. In this paragraph \(R[F(s)]=[F(1-s)]\) is the coefficient
reflection, so the ordered global degree-one mirror is \(-R\), not
\(R\). Set \[
\mathsf V_a=aT_{a^{-1}}=RT_aR.
\tag{SDT8.13}
\] On \(\mathcal B\), reflection satisfies
\(b_{R_0,M}(F(1-s))\le b_{R_0+1,M}(F)\); the different letter \(R_0\)
here is a strip width. The original functional equation preserves the
full multiplicities at \(\rho\) and \(1-\rho\), so reflection preserves
\(\mathcal I\). Both \(R\) and \(T_a\) therefore act continuously on
\(\mathcal Q\) and preserve the finite full-zero support, including the
reflected multiplicities. Equation (SDT8.9) at the parameter \(a^{-1}\),
with the prefactor \(a\) retained, gives \[
\iota(\mathsf V_aG)
=a\,a^{-1}(T_a)'\iota(G)
=(T_a)'\iota(G).
\tag{SDT8.14}
\] The operator \(\mathsf V_a\) is therefore continuous for (SDT8.11)
and extends to the actual ordinary transpose \(T_a'\) on its completion.
For the original action \(T_a\), the extension is instead
\(a(T_{a^{-1}})'\), exactly as in (SDT8.9).

There is also an unreflected residue map \[
\phi=\iota R,\qquad
\phi(G)(F)=\sum_\rho\operatorname{Res}_{s=\rho}
\frac{F(s)G(s)}{\zeta(s)}\,ds,\qquad
\phi T_a=(T_a)'\phi.
\tag{SDT8.15}
\] The middle formula substitutes \(RG(1-s)=G(s)\) before taking
residues, so it introduces no change-of-variable sign. The last identity
follows either directly by multiplying the integrand by \(a^s\), or from
\(RT_a=\mathsf V_aR\) and (SDT8.14).

Its exact topological receiver can be specified without assuming
continuity of \(R\) in an unexamined topology: equip
\(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}\) with \[
p_B^{\mathrm{unref}}(G)
=\sup_{F\in B}\left|
\sum_\rho\operatorname{Res}_{s=\rho}
\frac{F(s)G(s)}{\zeta(s)}\,ds\right|
=p_B^{\mathrm{res}}(RG).
\tag{SDT8.16}
\] Since \(R^2=1\) and
\(R\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}=\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}\), it is a
homeomorphism from this unreflected topology to the reflected topology
(SDT8.11). The map \(\phi\) has the same range
\(\mathscr D_{\mathrm{fin}}\), so its completion is also canonically
\(\mathcal Q'_\beta\), now intertwining \(T_a\) with the ordinary
transpose \(T_a'\). These are two explicitly related residue topologies;
neither has been silently substituted for the inherited topology of
\(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{fin}}\subset\mathcal Q\).

\section{SDT9. Exact implication and limits of this
calculation}\label{sdt9.-exact-implication-and-limits-of-this-calculation}

The proved chain is \[
\begin{array}{c}
\text{original weighted derivative estimates on }A\\
\Downarrow\ {\rm SDT2\text{--}SDT3}\\
\text{every bounded subset of }Q\text{ has compact closure}\\
\Downarrow\ {\rm SDT4\text{--}SDT5}\\
\text{compact lifts and exact bounded lifts through }q\\
\Downarrow\\
Q'_\beta\simeq J^\perp\subset A'_\beta,
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{c}
\text{bounded-compact property and the actual Fréchet topology}\\
\Downarrow\ {\rm SDT6}\\
(\mathcal Q'_\beta)'=\mathcal Q\\
\Downarrow\ {\rm SDT7}\\
\overline{\mathscr D_{\rm fin}}^{\,\beta}=\mathcal Q'_\beta.
\end{array}
\tag{SDT9.1}
\] The arrows name the exact proofs that justify the topology change.
The compact lift is the finite-choice series (SDT4.7), not a claimed
linear section. The dense space at the bottom right consists of
functionals, not finite-support classes in the primal quotient.

This establishes the full strong-dual cohomology topology for the actual
CDI coefficient complexes and strengthens their finite-jet detection to
uniform approximation on bounded subsets. It neither constructs a
Verdier dualizing sheaf nor identifies these infinite-dimensional
coefficient duals with a finite-rank étale receiver. No
weight-separation or RH conclusion is inferred from these topological
statements.

\section{CSD0. Input stage and the category being

The supporting datum remains
\(\tau\langle Z_1;\mathrm{no}\ Z_2\rangle\). All coefficient vector

For this continuation the current READ\_FIRST\_USER\_CONSTRUCTION.md,

The original-source use is that recorded in CSP0 and CDW0: Alain Connes

\section{CSD1. Full primal source and single
resolution}\label{csd1.-full-primal-source-and-single-resolution}

Let \(Y=\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)\), \(P=\{0,\infty\}\), and
\(i:P\hookrightarrow Y\). Retain \[
S=\{f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R;\mathbb C):f(-v)=f(v),\
f(0)=0,\ \int_{\mathbb R}f(v)\,dv=0\},\quad
V_\pm=S\oplus E_\pm,\quad E_\pm=\mathbb C^2,
\] \[
A=\left\{a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R_{>0}):
\sup_{u>0}(u^N+u^{-N})|(u\partial_u)^ja(u)|<\infty\
\text{for all }N,j\ge0\right\},
\] \[
\begin{gathered}
\Sigma f(u)=2\sum_{k\ge1}f(ku),\quad
Ra(u)=u^{-1}a(u^{-1}),\quad
\widehat f(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(v)e^{-2\pi ivt}\,dv,\\
\quad r_+(f,e)=\Sigma f,\quad r_-(h,e)=R\Sigma h=\Sigma\widehat h.
\end{gathered}
\tag{CSD1.1}
\] The last equality uses the full Poisson formula with terms
\(u^{-1}h(0)-\int h\), which vanish on this stated \(S\). Both
coordinates of each \(E_\pm\), labelled value at zero and real integral,
remain distinct.

The actual source image \(J=\Sigma S\) is closed, \(\Sigma:S\to J\) is a
topological isomorphism, and \(Q=A/J\) has its Fréchet quotient
topology. The proved inverse-image sheaf is \[
\mathscr F=\pi^{-1}\Omega
=\underline A_Y\times_{i_*(A\oplus A)}i_*(V_+\oplus V_-).
\tag{CSD1.2}
\] Here \(\pi(0)=x_+\), \(\pi(\infty)=x_-\), and
\(\pi(\mathbb C^\times)=\eta\). Its generic inverse image is the entire
punctured plane, not a numerical coordinate assigned to \(\tau\).

Put \(V=V_+\oplus V_-\). The difference map is onto on stalks through
its evaluation component and gives \[
0\to\mathscr F\to\underline A_Y\oplus i_*V
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ev}-r}i_*A^2\to0.
\tag{CSD1.3}
\] For smooth \(A\)-valued differential forms \(\mathscr E_A^q\), the
single resolution from CDW2 is \[
\mathscr K^0=\mathscr E_A^0\oplus i_*V,\quad
\mathscr K^1=\mathscr E_A^1\oplus i_*A^2,\quad
\mathscr K^2=\mathscr E_A^2,
\] \[
d^0(f,v)=(df,\mathrm{ev}(f)-rv),\qquad d^1(\omega,a)=d\omega.
\tag{CSD1.4}
\] Its degree-zero kernel is (CSD1.2). At a pole, a closed pair
\((\omega,a)\) has primitive \(f=g+a-g(p)\), \(v=0\), where
\(dg=\omega\). Away from the poles the coefficient-valued Poincaré lemma
applies. This proves exactness in positive degrees with continuous local
primitives. Forms and finite skyscrapers are fine.

This resolution also computes compactly supported cohomology. A section
defined near a compact set extends after multiplication by a smooth
cutoff equal to one on a smaller neighborhood of that set. The
partition-of-unity contraction of the augmented Čech complex therefore
works with compact supports: only finitely many members of a locally
finite partition meet an input compact support, and all multiplications
and sums are continuous. This proves the needed compact-support
acyclicity for these form and skyscraper terms. It does not imply
acyclicity for sections supported at a single point.

\section{CSD2. Continuous compact-support
contraction}\label{csd2.-continuous-compact-support-contraction}

Set \(\mathcal E_c^q(U;A)=\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr E_A^q)\). Its topology is
the locally convex inductive limit over compact supports, each given all
smooth-derivative seminorms from \(A\). Finite pole sums have their
product topologies. Extension by zero of compactly supported forms is
continuous.

An explicit compact-support Poincaré calculation is useful. In an
oriented plane chart choose \(\rho_x,\rho_y\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\)
with integrals one. Define \[
I_x f(y)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)\,dx,\qquad
H_x f(x,y)=\int_{-\infty}^x f(t,y)\,dt
-\left(\int_{-\infty}^x\rho_x(t)\,dt\right)I_x f(y),
\tag{CSD2.1}
\] and define \(H_y\) similarly. Completeness of \(A\) supplies the
integrals. For every continuous seminorm, \[
p\!\left(\int f\right)\le\int p(f),
\tag{CSD2.2}
\] which also proves continuity after any fixed number of derivatives.

For compactly supported forms put \[
K(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=H_xP,
\] \[
K(G\,dx\wedge dy)=H_xG\,dy-\rho_x(x)H_y(I_xG)(y)\,dx,
\qquad K|_{\mathcal E_c^0}=0.
\tag{CSD2.3}
\] Each output is supported in a fixed rectangle determined by the input
support and the two fixed bumps. Thus these are continuous operators on
the stated inductive limits. Direct differentiation gives \[
Kd f=f,\qquad dK\omega+Kd\omega=\omega\quad(\deg\omega=1),
\] \[
dK\omega=\omega-\rho_x\rho_y\,dx\wedge dy
\int_{\mathbb R^2}\omega\quad(\deg\omega=2).
\tag{CSD2.4}
\] Indeed \(\partial_xH_xf=f-\rho_xI_xf\) and \(H_y\partial_yg=g\) for
compactly supported \(g\) give every term in these identities. The bump
two-form has positive integral one and is annihilated by \(K\). This is
a continuous contraction onto \(A\) in degree two. An
orientation-preserving disk-to-plane diffeomorphism transfers it to
every disk below.

On the cylinder \(t=\log|z|\), \(\theta=\arg z\), combine the
one-dimensional compact contraction in \(t\) with the following circle
homotopy: subtract the angular mean, integrate that mean-zero
coefficient from zero to \(\theta\), then subtract the mean of the
primitive. Its derivative is the original coefficient minus its mean and
it is periodic. The surviving circle classes are constants and
\(d\theta/(2\pi)\). The compact cylinder classes are consequently \[
\rho(t)\,dt\quad(\deg1),\qquad
\rho(t)\,dt\wedge\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}\quad(\deg2),\qquad \int\rho=1.
\tag{CSD2.5}
\] All homotopies are continuous and use actual test forms, not an
unproved homotopy-invariance assertion for topological coefficients.

\section{CSD3. The continuous-current
sheaf}\label{csd3.-the-continuous-current-sheaf}

For \(-2\le n\le0\), define \[
\mathscr T_A^n(U)=\bigl(\mathcal E_c^{-n}(U;A)\bigr)',
\qquad (dT)(\phi)=(-1)^{n+1}T(d\phi).
\tag{CSD3.1}
\] Other degrees vanish. Each dual may carry the weak topology of
pointwise evaluation or the strong topology of uniform convergence on
bounded test sets. Both use exactly the same continuous functionals.

Restriction is transpose to extension by zero. To prove the sheaf axiom,
decompose a compactly supported test form by a locally finite
subordinate partition of unity and evaluate compatible local functionals
on its pieces. Only finitely many terms meet the compact support.
Compatibility proves independence of the partition and uniqueness;
continuity on every fixed-support space proves continuity on the
specified inductive limit. Restriction and scalar multiplication of
currents are continuous for both dual topologies: they transpose
continuous operations on tests which take bounded sets to bounded sets.

The differential is the continuous Hom differential, so \(d^2=0\).
Smooth functions multiply currents on their test argument, making every
term a fine sheaf. This gives ordinary-section acyclicity on all opens
used below.

The positive complex orientation defines \[
\underline{A'}_Y[2]\longrightarrow\mathscr T_A^\bullet,\qquad
c_\lambda(\phi)=\int_U\lambda(\phi)
\quad(\phi\text{ a compactly supported two-form}).
\tag{CSD3.2}
\] It is continuous and closed by Stokes. Transpose the explicit
contraction (CSD2.4): this proves that (CSD3.2) is a local
quasi-isomorphism with continuous inverse on cohomology. In particular
its coefficient is the entire continuous \(A'\). The weak-topology
comparison is a homeomorphism. For this local coefficient the
strong-topology comparison also follows from the two explicit
bounded-set preserving test maps.

No tensor-product identification between scalar distributions and \(A'\)
is used. Currents mean exactly (CSD3.1). At a pole define the positive
Dirac current \[
\delta_p\lambda(f)=\lambda(f(p)),\qquad i_*A'\longrightarrow\mathscr T_A^0.
\tag{CSD3.3}
\] This is the actual local Gysin chain map, with its orientation fixed
below.

\section{CSD4. The actual support-dual
complex}\label{csd4.-the-actual-support-dual-complex}

Using the ordinary cone differential \(d(b,a)=(d_Bb+ga,-d_Aa)\), put \[
\boxed{\mathscr D_c\mathscr F
=\operatorname{Cone}\!\left(i_*A'^2
\xrightarrow{(\delta,-r')}
\mathscr T_A^\bullet\oplus i_*V'\right).}
\tag{CSD4.1}
\] The domain is in degree zero. Its complete terms and maps are \[
(\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)^{-2}=\mathscr T_A^{-2},\qquad
(\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)^{-1}=\mathscr T_A^{-1}\oplus i_*A'^2,\qquad
(\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)^0=\mathscr T_A^0\oplus i_*V',
\] \[
d^{-2}T=(dT,0),\qquad
d^{-1}(T,\lambda_+,\lambda_-)
=\left(dT+\delta_0\lambda_++\delta_\infty\lambda_-,
-r_+'\lambda_+,-r_-'\lambda_-\right).
\tag{CSD4.2}
\] Every map is continuous for both dual topologies.

The cone is the literal continuous transpose of the compact-support
resolution: for every open \(U\), \[
\boxed{\Gamma(U,\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)
=\bigl(\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr K^\bullet)\bigr)^\vee,\qquad
(C^\vee)^n=(C^{-n})',\quad
d^\vee_n=(-1)^{n+1}(d_C^{-n-1})'.}
\tag{CSD4.3}
\] For degree \(-1\), transposing \(d^0(f,v)\) gives
\(T(df)+\sum_p\lambda_p(f(p)-r_pv_p)\), exactly (CSD4.2). Degree \(-2\)
has the minus sign in (CSD3.1). Restriction in (CSD4.3) is adjoint to
extension by zero.

Evaluation is a cochain pairing: its two differential contributions are
\((-1)^{n+1}\lambda(dc)\) and \((-1)^n\lambda(dc)\), whose sum is zero.
Formula (CSD4.3), together with the proved compact-support resolution,
is the precise continuous support-duality meaning used here. It is an
actual sheaf complex, not a declaration that general continuous
dualization is exact.

Using (CSD3.2), it represents the candidate \[
\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(i_*A'^2
\xrightarrow{(\mathrm{Gys},-r')}
\underline{A'}_Y[2]\oplus i_*V'\bigr),
\tag{CSD4.4}
\] whose derived Gysin arrow is represented exactly by (CSD3.3).

\section{CSD5. Pole stalk and original compact-support
pairing}\label{csd5.-pole-stalk-and-original-compact-support-pairing}

Use the positive local coordinate \(z_p=z\) at zero and \(z_p=1/z\) at
infinity. The form \[
\vartheta_p=\frac{d\arg z_p}{2\pi}
\tag{CSD5.1}
\] is locally integrable. Its degree-minus-one current is
\(h_p\lambda(\phi)=\int\vartheta_p\wedge\lambda(\phi)\). The local
\(1/r\) coefficient is integrable against the area factor
\(r\,dr\,d\theta\). Stokes on a punctured disk with compact test \(f\)
gives \[
d(h_p\lambda)(f)=h_p\lambda(df)=\lambda(f(p)),
\qquad dh_p\lambda=\delta_p\lambda.
\tag{CSD5.2}
\] The positive small-circle limiting integral fixes the sign.

The primal pole costalk is
\(L_p=[V_p\xrightarrow{r_p}A\xrightarrow0 A]\) in degrees \(0,1,2\). Its
dual differential is \(r_p'\) in degrees \(-1,0\). The actual stalk
comparison is \[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{degree}&L_p^\vee\longrightarrow(\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)_p\\ \hline
-2&\lambda\mapsto c_\lambda\\
-1&\mu\mapsto(h_p\mu,-\mu)\\
0&\nu\mapsto(0,\nu).
\end{array}
\tag{CSD5.3}
\] Indeed \(d(h_p\mu,-\mu)=(0,r_p'\mu)\). The local current contraction
leaves only \(A'\) in degree \(-2\); the Dirac arrow is locally
null-homotopic through \(h_p\), leaving exactly \(r_p'\). This proves
the quasi-isomorphism with continuous maps. The same construction on
shrinking disks gives the actual stalk.

For a direct pairing check choose \(\chi\in C_c^\infty\) equal to one
near \(p\), and a compact positive two-form \(\omega_c\) of integral
one. The primal compact-source chain map is \[
L_p\longrightarrow\Gamma_c(U,\mathscr K),\quad
v\mapsto(\chi r_pv,v),\quad
a\text{ in degree1}\mapsto(d\chi\,a,0),\quad
a\text{ in degree2}\mapsto\omega_c a.
\tag{CSD5.4}
\] Its differential is \(r_p\). The compact contraction (CSD2.4)
followed by elimination of the evaluation coordinate proves it is a
quasi-isomorphism. Pairing it with (CSD5.3) gives \[
\lambda(a),\qquad
\int\vartheta_p\wedge d\chi\,\mu(a)=\mu(a),\qquad
\nu(v).
\tag{CSD5.5}
\] The middle identity is (CSD5.2) on test \(\chi\). This is precisely
CDI's positive-orientation costalk pairing.

For clarity about the cohomology topology, on each fixed disk \(U\),
transposing the compact-test map (CSD5.4) gives a continuous reverse
chain map from sections of the current complex on that disk. It is not
an evaluation of an arbitrary current germ on a fixed test support. In
degrees \(-2,-1,0\) it is \[
T\mapsto\bigl(a\mapsto T(\omega_c a)\bigr),\qquad
(T,\lambda)\mapsto\bigl(a\mapsto T(d\chi\,a)\bigr),
\] \[
(T,\nu)\mapsto\nu+r_p'\bigl(a\mapsto T(\chi a)\bigr).
\tag{CSD5.7}
\] It composes with the disk version of (CSD5.3) to the identity.
Because that map is already a quasi-isomorphism, the induced cohomology
maps are inverse continuous maps. Their cohomology identifications agree
under shrinking disks: degree-minus-two cocycles are constant currents;
for a degree-minus-one cocycle \((T,\lambda)\), the equation
\(dT+\delta_p\lambda=0\) gives \(T(d\chi\,a)=-\lambda(a)\), independent
of the cutoff; and degree-zero cutoff changes lie in
\(\operatorname{im}r_p'\). The underlying sheaf stalk therefore has
these groups. Its cohomology topology in this proof means the stable
small-disk cohomology topology, identified by these identity transition
maps. It is not a claim that arbitrary locally convex inductive limits
of germs commute with forming cohomology topologies. This gives the
precise topological comparison for both stated dual topologies before
identifying the quotient coefficient through SDT below.

Consequently \[
H^{-2}(i_p^*\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)=A',\quad
H^{-1}(i_p^*\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)=Q',\quad
H^0(i_p^*\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)=E_p'.
\tag{CSD5.6}
\] The middle identification is \(\ker r_p'=J^\perp=q'Q'\). The last
uses the actual splitting \(V_p=E_p\oplus J\) from \(\Sigma^{-1}\), and
Hahn--Banach extends every continuous functional on closed \(J\) to
\(A\). Thus these are the entire continuous duals.

\section{CSD6. Derived point support, computed
separately}\label{csd6.-derived-point-support-computed-separately}

Fineness does not make a current sheaf automatically acyclic for support
at a point. A current on a punctured disk need not extend across its
missing point. Compute support by the actual restriction fibre cone \[
R\Gamma_{\{p\}}(U,\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)
=\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(
\Gamma(U,\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)\to
\Gamma(U\setminus\{p\},\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)\bigr)[-1].
\tag{CSD6.1}
\] The ordinary sections here compute hypercohomology because the
displayed terms are fine. They are not replaced by termwise
point-supported currents.

On a disk the current complex has \(A'\) in degree \(-2\). On its
puncture it has \(A'\) in degrees \(-2,-1\), represented by
\(c_\lambda,h_p\lambda\), by the cylinder contraction (CSD2.5). In
particular \(h_p\lambda\) pairs as \(-\lambda(a)\) with
\(\rho(t)dt\,a\), since \(d\theta\wedge dt=-dt\wedge d\theta\). This
radial sign is retained.

Restriction on (CSD5.3) is identity in degrees \(-2,-1\) and zero in
degree zero. In the fibre-cone convention
\(d(x,y)=(dx,\mathrm{res}(x)-dy)\), cancel its contractible
degree-minus-two pair. The remaining complex is \[
A'\longrightarrow V_p'\oplus A',\qquad
\mu\longmapsto(r_p'\mu,\mu).
\tag{CSD6.2}
\] The last coordinate records the punctured angular current. The
positive supported coordinate is its negative: in the same cone,
\(d(h_p\lambda,0)=(\delta_p\lambda,h_p\lambda)\), so
\((\delta_p\lambda,0)\) is cohomologous to \((0,-h_p\lambda)\). Changing
to that positive supported coordinate and negating the source rewrites
(CSD6.2) as \[
A'\xrightarrow{\lambda\mapsto(\lambda,-r_p'\lambda)}
A'\oplus V_p'\quad\text{in degrees }-1,0.
\tag{CSD6.3}
\] The first target is now measured by the positive Dirac orientation.

The continuous deformation retraction onto \(V_p'[0]\) is \[
P(a,\nu)=\nu+r_p'a,\qquad S(\nu)=(0,\nu),\qquad h(a,\nu)=a.
\tag{CSD6.4}
\] One has \(PS=1\), \(hd=1\) on degree \(-1\), and
\(dh(a,\nu)=(a,-r_p'a)=(a,\nu)-SP(a,\nu)\). Therefore \[
\boxed{i_p^!\mathscr D_c\mathscr F\simeq V_p'[0]
=(i_p^*\mathscr F)^\vee.}
\tag{CSD6.5}
\] Costalk-to-stalk is \(\nu\mapsto(0,\nu)\) in (CSD5.3); on degree-zero
cohomology it is restriction \(V_p'\to E_p'\). Together with CSD5 this
proves both support/stalk comparisons from actual local complexes.

\section{CSD7. Global angular current and the CDI chain
comparison}\label{csd7.-global-angular-current-and-the-cdi-chain-comparison}

The angular form \(\vartheta=d\arg z/(2\pi)\) is locally integrable on
the sphere. At infinity it is \(-\vartheta_-\); hence \[
d(\vartheta\lambda)=\delta_0\lambda-\delta_\infty\lambda.
\tag{CSD7.1}
\] The original global complex and its continuous dual are \[
D=[V_+\oplus V_-\xrightarrow{r_+-r_-}A\xrightarrow0 A],
\] \[
D^\vee=[A'\xrightarrow0 A'
\xrightarrow{\mu\mapsto(r_+'\mu,-r_-'\mu)}
V_+'\oplus V_-']
\tag{CSD7.2}
\] in degrees \(0,1,2\) and \(-2,-1,0\), respectively. There is an
actual continuous chain map \[
\Psi:D^\vee\longrightarrow\Gamma(Y,\mathscr D_c\mathscr F),
\] \[
\lambda\mapsto c_\lambda\quad(\deg-2),\qquad
\mu\mapsto(\vartheta\mu;-\mu,+\mu)\quad(\deg-1),\qquad
(\nu_+,\nu_-)\mapsto(0;\nu_+,\nu_-)\quad(\deg0).
\tag{CSD7.3}
\] The middle differential's current terms cancel by (CSD7.1), leaving
precisely \((r_+'\mu,-r_-'\mu)\).

To prove this is a quasi-isomorphism, compute the global current complex
using the local and cylinder contractions (CSD2.4)--(CSD2.5) and
two-chart Mayer--Vietoris. Its cohomology is \(A'\) in degrees \(-2,0\)
and zero in degree \(-1\). The first class is \(c_\lambda\); the last is
evaluated on constant test functions. Both positive Dirac currents have
that last value \(\lambda\). All comparisons are finite sums, the
written integral operators and partition-of-unity maps, so they are
continuous. This computes the current cohomology without assuming
arbitrary exactness of continuous dualization.

The cone then has the finite model \[
P^{-2}=A',\quad P^{-1}=A'^2,\quad
P^0=A'\oplus V_+'\oplus V_-',
\] \[
d^{-1}(\lambda_+,\lambda_-)
=(\lambda_++\lambda_-,-r_+'\lambda_+,-r_-'\lambda_-).
\tag{CSD7.4}
\] Its explicit deformation retraction is \[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{degree}&P\to D^\vee&D^\vee\to P\\ \hline
-2&1&1\\
-1&(\lambda_+,\lambda_-)\mapsto-\lambda_+&
\mu\mapsto(-\mu,\mu)\\
0&(a,\nu_+,\nu_-)\mapsto(\nu_+,\nu_-+r_-'a)&
(\nu_+,\nu_-)\mapsto(0,\nu_+,\nu_-).
\end{array}
\tag{CSD7.5}
\] The homotopy \(h^0(a,\nu_+,\nu_-)=(0,a)\) satisfies \(dh+hd=1-SP\);
substitute into (CSD7.4) to check both degrees. The current map (CSD7.3)
induces the section in (CSD7.5), proving its quasi-isomorphism.

There is also a direct pairing check. Set \[
\omega_Y=\frac1\pi\frac{dx\wedge dy}{(1+|z|^2)^2},\qquad \int_Y\omega_Y=1.
\] The primal finite complex maps into global sections of \(\mathscr K\)
by \[
(v_+,v_-)\mapsto
(\operatorname{constant}(r_-v_-),v_+,v_-),\quad
b\text{ in degree1}\mapsto(0;-b,0),\quad
a\text{ in degree2}\mapsto\omega_Ya.
\tag{CSD7.6}
\] Its differential is \(r_+-r_-\), including the displayed degree-one
minus. Pairing (CSD7.3) and (CSD7.6) gives the original evaluation in
every degree. Thus this realizes CDI's pairings and signs, not only its
cohomology groups.

The continuous transpose of (CSD7.6) is an explicit cohomological
inverse to (CSD7.3). Put \(\ell_T(a)=T(\operatorname{constant}(a))\) for
a degree-zero current. In degrees \(-2,-1,0\), this reverse chain map is
\[
T\mapsto\bigl(a\mapsto T(\omega_Ya)\bigr),\qquad
(T,\lambda_+,\lambda_-)\mapsto-\lambda_+,
\] \[
(T,\nu_+,\nu_-)\mapsto(\nu_+,\nu_-+r_-'\ell_T).
\tag{CSD7.8}
\] For degree \(-1\), its chain identity is
\((-r_+'\lambda_+,r_-'\lambda_+)=d_{D^\vee}(-\lambda_+)\). It composes
with \(\Psi\) to the identity in every degree. All test embeddings in
this formula are continuous and take bounded sets to bounded sets.
Therefore the induced inverse cohomology maps are continuous for both
weak and strong dual topologies. No theorem that continuous dualization
preserves arbitrary quasi-isomorphisms is used to prove this assertion.

In particular \[
H^{-2}(Y,\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)=A',\qquad
H^{-1}(Y,\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)=Q',\qquad
H^0(Y,\mathscr D_c\mathscr F)=Z',
\] \[
Z=\{(v_+,v_-):r_+v_+=r_-v_-\}\simeq J\oplus E_+\oplus E_-.
\tag{CSD7.7}
\] The last comparison uses the original Fourier-source inverse and
retains all four endpoint lines.

\section{CSD8. Restriction realizes the transposed support
map}\label{csd8.-restriction-realizes-the-transposed-support-map}

Restriction of the global angular current is \(h_+\) at zero and
\(-h_-\) at infinity. Thus (CSD7.3) and (CSD5.3) give exactly \[
D^\vee\to L_+^\vee:
\quad(\deg0,\deg-1,\deg-2)=(\operatorname{pr}_{V_+'},+1,+1),
\] \[
D^\vee\to L_-^\vee:
\quad(\deg0,\deg-1,\deg-2)=(\operatorname{pr}_{V_-'},-1,+1).
\tag{CSD8.1}
\] These are the transposes of the original support-to-global map \[
L_+\oplus L_-\to D,\quad
k^0=1,\quad k^1(b_+,b_-)=b_+-b_-,\quad k^2(c_+,c_-)=c_++c_-.
\tag{CSD8.2}
\] Consequently degree-minus-one is anti-diagonal and degree-minus-two
diagonal: \[
Q'\to Q'^2:\mu\mapsto(\mu,-\mu),\qquad
A'\to A'^2:\lambda\mapsto(\lambda,\lambda).
\tag{CSD8.3}
\] Degree zero is endpoint restriction \(Z'\to E_+'\oplus E_-'\).

The complete cone comparison is \[
\operatorname{Cone}(k)^\vee
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Cone}(k^\vee)[-1],\qquad
(\phi,\psi)\mapsto((-1)^{n+1}\psi,\phi)\text{ in degree }n.
\tag{CSD8.4}
\] Substitution into the Hom and shifted-cone differentials proves it is
a chain isomorphism. The dual long row is therefore the full CDI5 row \[
0\to A'\xrightarrow{\Delta}A'^2
\xrightarrow{-\lambda_++\lambda_-}A'
\xrightarrow0Q'\xrightarrow{(\mu,-\mu)}Q'^2
\xrightarrow{q'(\mu_++\mu_-)}A'
\xrightarrow{r'}Z'\to E_+'\oplus E_-'\to0.
\tag{CSD8.5}
\] Here \(r:Z\to A\) is common restriction and
\(r'\lambda=(\lambda|_J,0,0)\) in (CSD7.7). Diagonal/difference
identities and Hahn--Banach on \(J\subset A\) prove exactness. Thus the
earlier continuous coefficient duality has an actual sheaf support
construction realizing its maps.

The ordinary annular dual in (CSD8.4) has degrees \(-1,0\). It is not
confused with \(R\Gamma(\mathbb C^\times,\mathscr T_A)\), whose degrees
are \(-2,-1\) because it is dual to compactly supported annular
cohomology. Formula (CSD4.3) specifies the support convention.

\section{CSD9. Proper geometric transposes and both
mirrors}\label{csd9.-proper-geometric-transposes-and-both-mirrors}

A continuous coefficient-diagram map acts on compact tests and,
contravariantly, on this current complex. All evaluation comparisons are
natural for these actual transposes.

For a recovered positive integer \(n\), \(b_n(z)=z^n\) is proper. Hence
test pullback preserves compact supports and its transpose defines \[
(b_{n*}T)(\phi)=T(b_n^*\phi).
\tag{CSD9.1}
\] After including the transposed coefficient action, this is the proper
current pushforward
\(b_{n*}\mathscr D_c\mathscr F\to\mathscr D_c\mathscr F\), adjoint to
primal pullback. It is not pullback on the dual object and is not an
inverse root map.

The primal coefficient action is \[
T_ab(u)=b(u/a),\quad
\rho_+(a)(f,c_0,c_1)=(f(\cdot/a),c_0,ac_1),\quad
\rho_-(a)(h,d_0,d_1)=(ah(a\,\cdot),ad_0,d_1).
\tag{CSD9.2}
\] The current transpose uses \(T_n'\) and \(\rho_\pm(n)'\). Under
(CSD7.3) its complete finite-model action is \[
(nT_n',\,T_n',\,\rho_+(n)'\oplus\rho_-(n)')
\quad\text{in degrees }-2,-1,0.
\tag{CSD9.3}
\] For a direct check, \(b_{n*}c_\lambda=nc_\lambda\),
\(b_{n*}\vartheta=\vartheta\), and \(b_{n*}\delta_p=\delta_p\). On the
punctured receiver the \(n\) inverse branches each contribute \(1/n\) of
the angular form to its trace. The locally integrable current equality
extends across the poles. These calculations verify the precise
current/global comparison. The broader geometric trace with other
coefficient conventions is a separate receiver map, not identified with
this one by terminology.

The specified mirrors and their sphere orientation degrees are \[
w(z)=-1/z,\quad\varepsilon_w=+1;\qquad
\alpha(z)=-1/\overline z,\quad\varepsilon_\alpha=-1.
\tag{CSD9.4}
\] Both transpose the pole swap and use \(R'\). For a current
represented by a form, proper pushforward acts as
\(\varepsilon_g(g^{-1})^*\) because the integration orientation is
fixed. Thus \[
g_*c_\lambda=\varepsilon_gc_\lambda,\qquad
g_*\vartheta=-\vartheta\quad(g=w,\alpha),
\tag{CSD9.5}
\] using \(w^*\vartheta=-\vartheta\), \(\alpha^*\vartheta=+\vartheta\).
The global dual actions are exactly \[
(\varepsilon_gR',-R',\text{dual pole swap})
\quad\text{in degrees }-2,-1,0.
\tag{CSD9.6}
\] At pole stalks each angular current uses its own positive coordinate.
Degree minus one is \(+R'\) with pole swap, while degree minus two is
\(\varepsilon_gR'\) with swap. Hence (CSD8.1) intertwines the mirrors
with all CDI7 signs.

The coefficient contragredient giving an invariant pairing is different.
On the already constructed cohomological representation extended to
\(a>0\), it is \[
(a^{-1}(T_{a^{-1}})',\ (T_{a^{-1}})',\
\rho_+(a^{-1})'\oplus\rho_-(a^{-1})').
\tag{CSD9.7}
\] It satisfies
\(\langle B_a^\vee\lambda,B_ax\rangle=\langle\lambda,x\rangle\). This is
CDI6's inverse-parameter coefficient operation. It is not asserted to
arise from a holomorphic \(z^{1/a}\) and is not substituted for
(CSD9.1).

There is now also a separately constructed weighted trace on the primal
sheaf. GTR2 uses the sum over all \(n\) interior sheets and \(n\) times
the identity on each ramified pole space, including both endpoint
coordinates. It proves \(\operatorname{Tr}_n b_n^*=n\,1\) on that sheaf.
GTR3--GTR4 prove its global degree factors \((n,n,1)\), and, after
composing with the inverse coefficient action, the representative \[
\mathsf U_n=(n\rho(n^{-1}),\,nT_{n^{-1}},\,T_{n^{-1}}),
\qquad
\mathsf U_n\mathsf B_n=\mathsf B_n\mathsf U_n=n\,1
\tag{CSD9.8}
\] in primal degrees \(0,1,2\), where \(\rho=\rho_+\oplus\rho_-\). Its
transpose on the full coefficient dual consequently is \[
\mathsf U_n'
=(T_{n^{-1}}',\,nT_{n^{-1}}',\,n\rho(n^{-1})')
=n(\mathsf B_n^{-1})'
\tag{CSD9.9}
\] in degrees \(-2,-1,0\). These are the induced maps and the explicitly
constructed coefficient representative from GTR, not a claim that a
chain lift to currents is uniquely determined by its cohomology. In
particular the middle operator \(nT_{n^{-1}}'\) in (CSD9.9) is different
from \(T_n'\) in the current pushforward (CSD9.3). GTR5 proves that the
original reflected residue map intertwines the former operator. The
current support-duality comparison keeps these maps distinct and retains
the ramification factor.

\section{CSD10. Topologies and the proved extent of
duality}\label{csd10.-topologies-and-the-proved-extent-of-duality}

Every current and functional is continuous for the actual Fréchet and
compact-test topologies. The comparisons use explicit integrations,
cutoffs and continuous finite operations. Exactness of continuous
dualization for arbitrary locally convex complexes has not been assumed.

The weak-dual cohomology topologies are precisely CDI3's. The
annihilator \(J^\perp\subset A'\) has the weak topology of \(Q'\):
evaluation at \(a\) is evaluation at \(q(a)\), and every quotient vector
has a representative. The actual continuous decompositions
\(V_p=E_p\oplus J\) and \(V_+\oplus V_-=Z\oplus J\) transpose to finite
decompositions, identifying the degree-zero quotient topologies. The
current homotopies and comparison maps preserve those identifications.
All these pairings are separated and involve the entire continuous dual.

For strong duals every displayed map remains continuous. The induced
topology on \(Q'\subset A'_\beta\) initially has the seminorm family \[
\mu\longmapsto\sup_{a\in B}|\mu(q(a))|,
\qquad B\subset A\text{ bounded}.
\tag{CSD10.1}
\] The accepted SDT2--SDT5 proof now identifies this family with the
full strong topology of \(Q'\). It proves compact closure of every
bounded subset of \(Q\) using the original two-sided weighted derivative
bounds, then constructs a compact lift through \(q\) as a uniformly
convergent series of finite choices. Intersecting that compact lift with
the inverse image of a bounded subset \(B\subset Q\) gives a bounded set
\(\widetilde B\subset A\) with \(q(\widetilde B)=B\). Hence \[
\sup_{y\in B}|\mu(y)|=\sup_{a\in\widetilde B}|q'\mu(a)|,
\qquad
Q'_\beta\xrightarrow[\ q'\ ]{\ \sim\ }J^\perp\subset A'_\beta.
\tag{CSD10.2}
\] Conversely, continuous \(q\) takes bounded subsets of \(A\) to
bounded subsets of \(Q\), giving the other topology inclusion.

The finite source splittings used above give the strong topology on the
degree-zero groups, and the fixed-test maps (CSD5.7) and (CSD7.8)
identify the current cohomology topologies with those of the finite
coefficient complexes. Thus the global identifications are strong
topological isomorphisms with \(A'_\beta,Q'_\beta,Z'_\beta\). The pole
stalk groups, equipped with the stable small-disk cohomology topology
specified in CSD5, are strongly topologically isomorphic to
\(A'_\beta,Q'_\beta,E_p'{}_\beta\). The supported comparison (CSD6.4)
uses continuous finite operations on the local restriction cone and
gives \(V_p'{}_\beta\) with the analogous stable local topology. This
imports exactly SDT's proved bounded-lift result; it does not assume or
assert strong openness of the separate restriction
\(A'_\beta\to J'_\beta\).

Ordinary algebraic sheaf Hom is not invoked to turn these continuous
duals into algebraic duals. The exact support-dual object established
here is (CSD4.1), with test-functional characterization (CSD4.3) and its
proved local/global comparisons.

\section{CSD11. Original zeta and every coefficient
contribution}\label{csd11.-original-zeta-and-every-coefficient-contribution}

Neither \(A\) nor its original source \(J\) has changed. Retain \[
\Theta a(s)=\frac12\int_0^\infty a(u)u^s\,\frac{du}{u},\qquad
\mathcal M_0\Sigma f(s)=2\zeta(s)\int_0^\infty f(v)v^s\,\frac{dv}{v}
\quad(\Re s>1).
\tag{CSD11.1}
\] For \(f_0(v)=\frac\pi2v^2(2\pi v^2-3)e^{-\pi v^2}\), \[
\Theta\Sigma f_0(s)=F_0(s)
=\frac{s(s-1)}8\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s).
\tag{CSD11.2}
\] The endpoint values \(F_0(0)=F_0(1)=1/8\) and all trivial-zero
comparisons remain \[
F_0(-2r)=\frac{r(2r+1)(-1)^r\pi^r}{2\,r!}\zeta'(-2r)
=\frac{(1+2r)(2r)}8\pi^{-(1+2r)/2}
\Gamma((1+2r)/2)\zeta(1+2r),\quad r\ge1.
\tag{CSD11.3}
\] The complete inverse and these contributions are proved in SSI/ESI
and retained in CSP11/CDW10.

For \(\mathcal B\), the entire functions rapidly decreasing on every
bounded real strip, let \[
\mathcal I=\{F\in\mathcal B:F^{(j)}(\rho)=0
\text{ for every actual nontrivial zero }\rho,\ 0\le j<m_\rho\}.
\] The proved map is the topological isomorphism
\(\kappa:Q\to\mathcal Q=\mathcal B/\mathcal I\),
\(\kappa([a])=[\Theta a]\), with \(\Theta J=\mathcal I\). Its actual
continuous transpose is \[
\kappa':\mathcal Q'\to Q',\qquad
(\kappa'\lambda)([a])=\lambda([\Theta a]).
\tag{CSD11.4}
\] Thus the factor \(1/2\) has not disappeared in duality. Every jet
\(\delta_{\rho,j}([a])=(\Theta a)^{(j)}(\rho)\) is a continuous element
of the \(Q'\) in CSD5 and CSD7. Its entire transpose matrix is \[
T_a'\delta_{\rho,j}
=a^\rho\sum_{\ell=0}^j\binom j\ell
(\log a)^{j-\ell}\delta_{\rho,\ell}.
\tag{CSD11.5}
\] For the normal contragredient the scalar is \(a^{-\rho-1}\) and each
logarithm is \(-\log a\), as in CDI6.8. Every multiplicity is retained
without presuming a location inside the known open critical strip.

The notation in (CSD11.5) uses raw derivatives. GTR and RD also use
Taylor-coefficient functionals. Their exact comparison is \[
\delta_{\rho,j}^{\mathrm{raw}}
=j!\,\delta_{\rho,j}^{\mathrm{Taylor}},
\qquad
\delta_{\rho,j}^{\mathrm{Taylor}}([a])
=\frac{(\Theta a)^{(j)}(\rho)}{j!}.
\tag{CSD11.6}
\] In that latter basis the actual transfer transpose from (CSD9.9) is
\[
\mathsf U_n'\delta_{\rho,j}^{\mathrm{Taylor}}
=n^{1-\rho}\sum_{h=0}^j
\frac{(-\log n)^{j-h}}{(j-h)!}
\delta_{\rho,h}^{\mathrm{Taylor}}.
\tag{CSD11.7}
\] Multiplying by \(j!\) gives the raw-derivative formula with
\(\binom jh\). Thus the factorials, inverse parameter and ramification
factor are all explicit in the comparison to GTR.

This construction does not promote the finite-residue identification to
a topological self-duality of all \(Q\), replace \(J\) by \(Q\), or
infer positivity of a Hermitian form from separated evaluation.

\section{CSD12. Constructed support-duality
result}\label{csd12.-constructed-support-duality-result}

The actual sheaf complex (CSD4.1) is the continuous current dual of the
compact-support resolution. Its Gysin and endpoint arrow is
\((\delta,-r')\). The local angular current and restriction fibre cone
prove \[
i_p^*\mathscr D_c\mathscr F\simeq(i_p^!\mathscr F)^\vee,\qquad
i_p^!\mathscr D_c\mathscr F\simeq(i_p^*\mathscr F)^\vee.
\] The global chain map (CSD7.3) realizes CDI's entire continuous dual
of the original sphere complex. Its restrictions give the full diagonal
and anti-diagonal support maps. Proper cover transposes and both actual
mirrors retain their degree and orientation factors.

This proves continuous support duality for the specified receiver. It
assigns no operation to \(\tau\), introduces no finite-dimensional
coefficient replacement, and asserts no RH or Deligne-purity conclusion.

\section{GTR0. Construction stage and
sources}\label{gtr0.-construction-stage-and-sources}

The support remains \(\tau\langle Z_1;\mathrm{no}\ Z_2\rangle\). The
